text:
emily: Heads-up from the sample-app workshop: saw a weird interaction between generator streaming backpressure and context deadlines that made the stream never terminate in our minimal repro. filing here.

emily: Scenario: start a streaming Generator, read a chunk, then parent context has a short deadline. when deadline hits we cancel, but the generator goroutine blocks waiting on send to an internal buffer and never sees ctx.Done.

emily: Minimal repro:
```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 25*time.Millisecond)
iter, _ := client.Generator(ctx, req)
_ = iter.Next() // get first piece
// wait for deadline to fire and expect goroutines to unwind
time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
// check for leaked goroutines in test
```

raj: Is this with Generator.Stream (push) or Generator.Iter (pull)? backpressure behaviour differs.

emily: Stream (we used the streaming callback demo in the quickstart). but we also saw similar with Iter when the local buffer hits capacity.

tina: Ok that rings a bell: streaming writer tries to send into a buffered channel inside the SDK. if ctx.Done is checked only around network reads but not around `chan <- msg` it can deadlock if receiver side is blocked by slow consumer + deadline.

emily: Exactly. In our sample app the UI was rate-limited so consumer slowed down. Should the SDK prefer non-blocking select with ctx.Done on channel sends?

raj: We debated non-blocking vs blocking in earlier design: blocking preserves ordering and backpressure semantics for ml workloads. Non-blocking would drop tokens which is not acceptable for some uses.

tina: We might add an optional policy: `OnBackpressure: Block | DropOldest | BufferWithTimeout` as part of the GeneratorOptions. That gives explicit control and helps onboarding: demo app can use BufferWithTimeout to avoid leaks.

emily: That would solve the sampleapp friction. Also we need clearer docs: "if your consumer may block, use BufferWithTimeout or explicit Stop/ForceStop". Right now onboarding doc only mentions "call cancel" which is insufficient.

raj: From an implementation angle, we should ensure all internal goroutines select on the root ctx (not a copied one) and that channel sends use: `select { case ch <- v: case <-ctx.Done(): return }`. That fixes leak without changing visible semantics.

tina: Agree. small fix: make sure auth refresher and retry loops also use the passed-in ctx for cancellation. saw a different repro where auth's retry kept stream alive until a token refresh succeeded.

emily: Another DX item: parity with Python/Node SDKs. Python generator has `aclose()` and a `timeout` arg on the async iterator. Go lacks explicit immediate-close API. We should aim for parity so examples map across languages.

raj: Proposal: add `iter.Stop()` which attempts graceful shutdown and `iter.ForceStop()` which cancels internal goroutines and closes channels immediately. Also add `GeneratorOpt{BackpressurePolicy: ...}`. I'll open a PR with a small test proving ctx propagation + select on send.

tina: For previous releases we avoided ForceStop because of potential resource loss, but if it's opt-in and documented as "may lose in-flight tokens" it's fine for dev/debugging and onboarding.

emily: Can we also add a sampleapp patch in examples/quickstart that shows BufferWithTimeout and ForceStop usage? that'll reduce onboarding friction.

raj: yep I'll include examples and a test that reproduces previous leak. I'll signpost Go version too; we've seen different scheduler timings across go1.20/1.21/1.22 so tests should be tolerant.

tina: FYI add a short blurb in the SDK README under "Streaming best practices" and mention commons pitfalls: slow consumer, deadlines, auth retries.

devex-bot: Issue created: DEX-4991 "gen stream backpressure + deadline -> goroutine leak" (assignee: raj) :white_check_mark:

emily: thanks! putting a note in the onboarding checklist so new devs don't hit this during the workshop. :thumbsup:
